day1.text: Hi, I'm Lira! The Sun flared (M1.6) and sent a plasma cloud our way.
day1.lesson: A plasma cloud takes a few days to reach the Moon, so we have time to prepare.

day2.text: An M2.2 flare and two more plasma clouds are flying at us.
day2.lesson: Each flare class (A, B, C, M, X) is 10 times stronger than the one before.

day3.text: An M2.1 flare, and Earth has a magnetic storm with northern lights!
day3.lesson: Earth has a magnetic shield, but the Moon has none.

day4.text: A quiet day: just a tiny C3.9 flare.
day4.lesson: Even on a quiet day, weak cosmic radiation reaches the Moon.

day5.text: The plasma clouds from April 17–18 are almost at the Moon!
day5.lesson: The plasma cloud flew 150 million km in about 4 days.

day6.text: Four M-class flares — the Sun is warming up!
day6.lesson: Flares explode in sunspots, where the magnetic field is tangled.

day7.text: An M3.6 flare and three new plasma clouds are coming.
day7.lesson: NASA scientists calculate when a plasma cloud will arrive.

day8.text: An M2.0 flare and one more plasma cloud — it will catch up with the others.
day8.lesson: A fast plasma cloud can catch up with a slow one.

day9.text: The Sun is a bit calmer: just an M1.3 flare.
day9.lesson: Flare light takes 8 minutes; a plasma cloud takes days.

day10.text: The plasma clouds are about to hit the Moon — good thing we knew in advance!
day10.lesson: One plasma cloud can weigh a billion tons.

day11.text: An M3.0 flare, and the batteries charge well in the sunshine.
day11.lesson: A lunar day lasts about 14 Earth days.

day12.text: The quietest day of the week — perfect for science!
day12.lesson: Regolith, the Moon's dust and pebbles, can shield a base from radiation.

day13.text: An M3.7 flare, and the Sun sinks toward the horizon.
day13.lesson: The Moon always shows the same side to Earth.

day14.text: An M9.5 flare — almost class X! Night is coming.
day14.lesson: An M9.5 flare is only a little weaker than X1.

day15.text: The lunar night has come: energy is low now.
day15.lesson: A lunar night lasts 14 days and gets as cold as −173 °C.

day16.text: An M2.7 flare, and a magnetic storm on Earth.
day16.lesson: Solar particles can reach the base even at night.

day17.text: The first X-class flare (X1.6)! Radio may go quiet tomorrow.

day18.text: The radio is noisy after the X flare, so no forecast.
day18.lesson: Flares "blind" the ionosphere, the layer radio signals travel through.

day19.text: Two X-class flares at once: X1.3 and X1.2!
day19.lesson: A big sunspot group can flare many times in a row.

day20.text: The plasma clouds are coming, plus an X4.5 flare!
day20.lesson: An X4.5 flare is about 4.5 times stronger than X1.

day21.text: An M8.2 flare and two big plasma clouds are flying straight at us.
day21.lesson: The giant sunspot group AR 3664 is 15 times wider than Earth.

day22.text: Two X1.0 flares from the giant sunspot!
day22.lesson: The Sun's activity rises and falls every 11 years, and 2024 is near the peak.

day23.text: A radiation storm is starting — particles at nearly light speed!
day23.lesson: Radiation storm particles pass through thin walls.

day24.text: The strongest magnetic storm in 20 years, and the radiation goes on!
day24.lesson: That night, people saw northern lights even in Ukraine.

day25.text: An X5.8 flare — the strongest yet, and the radiation storm goes on!
day25.lesson: The best radiation shield is a thick layer of regolith or water.

day26.text: An X1.0 flare, and Earth's storm is still echoing.
day26.lesson: During storms, scientists watch over satellites and power grids.

day27.text: A new radiation storm! Hang on, sunrise is close.
day27.lesson: Astronauts wear dosimeters that count radiation.

day28.text: An X8.7 flare — the strongest since 2017!
day28.lesson: The Sun turns about once a month, so the big sunspot is turning away.

day29.text: Sunrise! The Sun is back over the base, with an X3.4 flare.
day29.lesson: Leaving the Moon is easier: gravity here is 6 times weaker.

day30.text: Departure day, and the Sun is finally calm!
day30.lesson: All 30 days are real events from NASA DONKI, 2024.
